International Basketball Data in R: EuroLeague, FIBA and 40+ Leagues with hoopR

Saiem Gilani

Source: vignettes/articles/international-basketball-leagues.Rmd
international-basketball-leagues.Rmd

hoopR is not only the NBA and college basketball. It also reads the public data feeds of the EuroLeague, FIBA’s national-team and club competitions and dozens of domestic leagues on six continents: 682 functions in 35 function families in this version. This guide maps each league to its function prefix, says what data it offers, and shows the call pattern so you can go from “I want Spanish league play-by-play” to a data frame quickly.

The code below is not run when this site is built: these functions call live league websites, which can be slow, rate-limited or blocked from the cloud servers that build documentation. Run the examples on your own machine. New to hoopR? Start with Getting Started with hoopR.

How are the international functions organized?

Three patterns cover almost everything:

  1. League families named after the league or its data provider: acb_*() for Spain’s Liga Endesa, kbl_*() for Korea, lba_*() for Italy, and so on. Each family has its own identifiers (match ids, game keys, round ids), so you usually start from a schedule function and pass its ids to the game functions.
  2. Platform families for data providers that power many leagues: genius_*() (Genius Sports, pick the league with org), atrium_*() (Sportradar Atrium, pick the site with website_id), nbl_rosetta_*() (the Australian NBL’s stats API, pick org) and fiba_gdap_*() (FIBA’s data platform, pick the competition with comp).
  3. Competition shortcuts that wrap a platform for one league with a common set of verbs, typically *_schedule(), *_pbp(), *_shots(), *_player_box() and *_team_box(): fiba_wc_*() for the World Cup, slb_*() for the UK’s Super League Basketball, lnb_*() for France, and more. They take an END-year season (2026 = 2025-26), like the rest of hoopR.

Every family is listed in the International Basketball and Euroleague Data sections of the reference, with a return-column table on each function page.

Which leagues are covered?

“pbp” is play-by-play, “shots” is shot locations, “box” is player and team box scores.

“no” means hoopR has no dedicated function for that data type in the family, not that the league never publishes it. Coverage by season varies by league and provider; check each function’s reference page.

How do I get EuroLeague data?

The EuroLeague family wraps the keyless Competition Engine and live APIs. competition_code is "E" for the EuroLeague and "U" for the EuroCup, and season_code is the competition code plus the season’s start year: "E2025" is the 2025-26 EuroLeague.

library(hoopR)
library(dplyr)

games <- euroleague_games(competition_code = "E", season_code = "E2025")

# game_code comes from the schedule
pbp   <- euroleague_game_pbp(game_code = 1, season_code = "E2025")
box   <- euroleague_game_boxscore(game_code = 1, season_code = "E2025")
shots <- euroleague_game_points(game_code = 1, season_code = "E2025")

# points by team from the play-by-play
pbp |>
  filter(playtype %in% c("2FGM", "3FGM", "FTM")) |>
  count(codeteam, playtype)

EuroLeague shot locations (coord_x, coord_y) are centimeters with the hoop at the origin. sdvplotR::sdv_court_coords(shots, "coord_x", "coord_y", provider = "euroleague") converts them to meters on the FIBA court that sdvplotR::sdv_surface("fiba") and sportyR::geom_basketball("fiba") draw; see the shot chart article for plotting.

How do I get FIBA World Cup, Olympic and EuroBasket data?

FIBA’s data platform (GDAP) identifies each edition of a competition with a comp id: 208182 is the 2023 World Cup, for example. The competition shortcuts look the id up for you from an END-year season (for one-year events, the event year).

# Every World Cup edition the shortcut knows about
fiba_wc_editions()

wc     <- fiba_wc_schedule(season = 2023)
wc_pbp <- fiba_wc_pbp(game_id = wc$game_id[1], season = 2023)

# The same verbs for other competitions
fiba_oly_schedule(season = 2024)
fiba_bcl_schedule(season = 2025)

# Or go through GDAP directly with a comp id
fiba_gdap_schedule(comp = 208182)
fiba_gamepage_shots(game_id = 100720, comp = 208182)

How do I use the Genius Sports and Atrium platform families?

Many leagues publish through the same provider, so one family serves them all. Genius Sports leagues are chosen with org; list competitions first to find the comp_id of a season.

genius_competitions(org = "ESAKE")
genius_schedule(org = "CEBL", comp_id = 47852)

# Shortcuts resolve the competition for you
slb_schedule(season = 2026)        # Super League Basketball (UK)
bal_schedule(season = 2025)        # Basketball Africa League

Sportradar Atrium sites are chosen with website_id (12 is LNB France, 14 LNBP Mexico, 3 NBL1 Australia, 13 El Salvador, 22 Panama, 236 Austria, 326 Montenegro):

atrium_fixtures(website_id = 12)

# Shortcuts
lnb_schedule(season = 2026)
fixtures <- lnb_schedule(season = 2026)
lnb_pbp(fixture_id = fixtures$fixture_id[1])

Use args() on any shortcut to see its exact arguments; the identifiers each game function needs are columns of the matching schedule function.

Domestic league examples

Each family follows its source’s identifiers. A few starting points, taken from the reference examples:

# Spain: Liga Endesa (ACB)
acb_matchlist(match_id = 105401)
acb_pbp(match_id = 105401)
acb_shots(match_id = 105401)

# Australia: NBL on the Rosetta API
nbl_rosetta_matches(org = "nbl", season = 2026, season_type = "regular")

# Japan, Korea, China
bleague_schedule(season = 2026, tab = 1, month = 10, day = 4)
kbl_schedule(from_date = "20251101", to_date = "20251102")
cba_schedule_month(month = 12, year = 2025)

# Italy, Lithuania, Adriatic, Turkey
lba_calendar(championship_id = 602, round = 1)
lkl_results(season = 2026)
aba_calendar(season = 2026)
tbf_schedule(competition = "bsl", season = 2027, week = 1)

# Germany, Spain (FEB), Denmark, Belgium / Netherlands
scb_games(league = "bbl")
feb_schedule(group = 1, season = 2027)
sportality_schedule(season = 2026)
sportpress_schedule(season = 2026)

# Russia, Israel, Slovenia
vtb_league_matches(league_slug = "vtb", season = 2026)
ibba_games(board_id = 5, board_round = 1, season = 2026)
kzs_matches(competition_id = 579,
            date_from = "2025-10-01T00:00:00.000Z", date_to = "2025-10-31T23:59:59.000Z")

# Canada, East Asia, Taiwan
cebl_games(season = 2025)
easl_schedule(season = 2026)
pleague_schedule(season = 2025)
tpbl_games(season = 2026)

Tips for working with international feeds

  • Start from the schedule. Game functions need the provider’s own game id (match_id, game_code, gmkey, fixture_id, schedule_key, …), which the schedule returns.
  • Check the season convention. hoopR’s shortcuts use END-year seasons, but some source arguments are the source’s own codes (EuroLeague season_code = "E2025" is the season starting in 2025). The returned season column tells you which season you got.
  • Be polite. Loop over games slowly and cache results with saveRDS(); these are live websites, and several block bursts of requests or requests from cloud servers.
  • Some hosts are unofficial. EASL and P. LEAGUE+ are read through third-party hosts, as the reference notes, and can disappear without notice.
  • Box-score metrics still apply. International box scores work with the league-agnostic helpers (nba_possessions(), nba_true_shooting_pct(), nba_four_factors()) once you rename columns; FIBA games are 40 minutes, so quote pace per 40. See the advanced metrics article.
